newsitem.title: USA: California city reaches out to Cuba.
newsitem.headline: California city reaches out to Cuba.

text.p: Cuba has a new ally in the United States -- Oakland, California.
The northern California city, often at the centre of controversy, wrote to government officials in Santiago de Cuba in January, suggesting they become so-called "friendship cities."
This week, Oakland received word that the Cubans had accepted the offer, city officials said on Thursday.
"It's basically a done deal," said Lewis Cohen, a spokesman for Oakland city council member Ignacio de la Fuente. "We've given our blessing to the effort and now just have to work out the specifics."
While it was not immediately clear what the partnership would involve, Cohen said it would include "cultural, educational and health exchanges."
Oakland is no stranger to controversy.
"We clearly go against the grain," Cohen said. "It's the hope of folks to be provocative."
In years past, Oakland has taken on apartheid and declared itself a "city of refuge" for people fleeing Latin America.

Last year the Oakland council barred the city from doing business with companies that operate in Burma, and the Oakland school board sparked a national debate by recognising so-called black English, or Ebonics, in the classroom.
Once the details are worked out, Oakland plans to send a delegation to visit Santiago de Cuba and may try to arrange a California visit for its Cuban counterparts, Cohen said.

Oakland Mayor Elihu Harris said the city, which opposes Washington's three decade-old economic embargo on Cuba, hopes the "friendship city" activities with Santiago de Cuba will improve relations between the countries.
"The city is not attempting to engage in foreign policy," Harris said. "We're trying to establish contact and communication. We're extending a hand of friendship."

Harris' Cuban counterpart, the president of the municipal assembly of Santiago de Cuba, welcomed Oakland's offer in a letter delivered to the Oakland city council earlier this week along with a box of Cuban cigars and a bottle of Cuban rum.

In the letter, President Nicolas Carbonel Igarza said establishing ties with Oakland would "allow the two peoples to get to know one another" and could be used to "educate people about the injustice" of the U.S. embargo.
